title: QPS imbalance tailcase scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
- Quick scratchpad to capture an odd tail phenomenon when QPS is "imbalanced" across request types (many tiny reqs + fewer heavy/generative requests). Trying to reproduce and capture mitigation leads.

Background / why I care:
- Product traffic mix shows ~87% short completion (<=16 tokens) and 13% long streaming requests (>256 tokens). Host-level QPS looks fine, but p99/p999 for long requests spikes during short-request bursts. Customers notice intermittent long tail.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Small requests keep filling batching slots and cause long-request tokens to wait for batch formation -> long tail.
2) KV-cache and warm-cache priming differ between request types; long requests miss cached prefixes and add latency.
3) Scheduler preemption/priority lanes currently too coarse -> slow-stealing of capacity for long runs.

Environment (quick):
- binary: rdinfer-server v1.12.0-rc3 (local dev build)
- model: open-opus-7b-8k (float16, q4f16 candidate) running on a4x (4x A100 80GB equiv in infra sim)
- runtime flags: --batch-window-ms=8 --max-batch-tokens=4096 --prefer-latency=false --kv-cache=true
- test driver: synthetic-driver v0.3 (custom) with per-type arrival control

Workloads tested (simplified):
- Mix A: 90% small (S) / 10% large (L) @ total QPS 200 (S=180 qps, L=20 qps)
- Mix B: 95% S / 5% L @ total QPS 240 (S=228, L=12)
- Mix C: 60% S / 40% L @ total QPS 200 (S=120, L=80)
- Isolated L-only baseline @20 qps for reference

Commands run (approx):
- ./driver --mix S:180,L:20 --dist poisson --run 30m --collect traces.json
- ./rdinfer --flags(...) > server.log 2>&1 &

Key raw observations (aggregated per 10s windows):
- Baseline L-only @20 qps: p50=62ms p95=118ms p99=190ms
- Mix A (90/10 @200): p50(L)=140ms p95(L)=420ms p99(L)=1.42s  (note: S latencies ~18-45ms)
- Mix B (95/5 @240): p50(L)=180ms p95(L)=650ms p99(L)=2.1s
- Mix C (60/40 @200): p50(L)=75ms p95(L)=160ms p99(L)=240ms

Immediate inference from numbers:
- Heavy skew toward small requests drastically increases tail for the long requests. When large proportion of S is high, long requests experience queuing/batching delays sometimes ballooning >2s.
- When L fraction is higher (Mix C) the scheduler is able to form more L-dedicated batches and p99 drops near baseline.

Detailed signals explored in traces.json (notes):
- Queue timestamps: long requests often sat queued waiting for batch-window expiration while small requests continuously filled new batches (batch composition: mostly S).
- Batch meta: observed batches where a long request sat as the single L but batch size kept growing with S until hitting max-window -> L waited ~8-60ms + token generation delay; but worst-case was when S arrival created many small batches and long reqs couldn't form their own batch => forced to wait across multiple batch cycles (accumulated wait >1s in some traces).
- KV cache hit: L requests frequently had cold prefixes (session starts), so extra decoder steps + cache population added ~30-80ms.
- CPU affinitization: no isolation between lanes; kernel scheduling caused preemption in heavy burst windows.

Quick micro-experiments (single-run changes):
1) Per-type min-batch-size: force L to have dedicated lane with min-batch-size=1 and max-delay-ms=2 -> p99(L) reduced from 1.42s to ~280ms in Mix A.
2) Priority lane + preempt: allow L to preempt S batches when waiting >80ms -> p99(L) ~260-300ms but S p95 increased slightly (from 42ms to 60ms).
3) Increase batch-window-ms to 20ms (more coalescing) -> overall throughput slightly better, but L tail worse (more S accumulation before L gets service).
4) KV-prefetch: for L requests, send a small prefetch request for first 64 tokens to populate KV (simulated) -> ~70ms improvement on median L in many runs but didn't fully solve p99 as queuing dominated.

Rough per-run summary (Mix A):
- default: p99 L = 1.42s
- dedicated-lane(min-delay=2ms): p99 L = 0.28s
- priority-preempt: p99 L = 0.30s
- kv-prefetch + dedicated-lane: p99 L = 0.22s

Cost/throughput trade-off notes:
- Dedicated lanes increase amortized tokens served for S slightly due to smaller effective batch utilization -> cost per-token up by ~4-6% in this simulation.
- Preemptive steals add jitter to S tail; might be acceptable if S SLA is looser.

Short ASCII timeline (example extract):
- t=0s: burst of S (80 qps for 10s) -> server forms small S batches (avg batch tokens 64)
- t=6s: L request arrives, sits waiting across 3 windows because S kept filling -> L start gen at t=6.52s -> end at t=7.1s

Quick conclusions / recommended mitigations to prototype upstream:
- Implement "typed lanes" in scheduler: small/fast vs large/slow, with configurable min batch and max-wait per type. This gives best p99 reduction with modest cost impact.
- Add a simple preemption threshold: if a request has been waiting > X ms and there is active S batch forming, allow stealing last N tokens from S batches to start L (or schedule immediate dedicated batch). Needs careful accounting.
- Expose a request-level hint (fastpath=true / preferred-lane=low-latency) so clients can mark important long calls. SDK default could mark streaming calls as high-priority.
- Improve KV-prefetch heuristics for new sessions (cheap prefetch for first k prefix tokens) to reduce decode overhead.

Next steps I want to run (short list):
- Reproduce Mix A with real model (closed-door) on dedicated infra (not sim) to validate numbers. (linked PERF-312)
- Try hybrid approach: per-type min-batch + kv-prefetch + circuit breaker to measure cost delta across production-like traces.
- Add better tracing in runtime to capture batch composition over time (timeline export per batch). Current trace format limited.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is acceptable S p95 regression if L p99 drops from >1s to ~250ms? Product input needed.
- Should lane assignment be static (per-route) or dynamic (learned from arrival patterns)? Dynamic is better but more complex.
- Do we want SDK hinting as first iteration to avoid runtime heuristics?

Random notes to self: 
- Diego to prototype scheduler patch in rdinfer-scheduler branch (PR above).
- Add a lightweight PR that introduces per-request priority header for testing in client.
- Keep an eye on memory amplification if we create too many dedicated micro-batches.

End of scratchpad.

(If revisiting: compare with "mixed-priority-warm-cache-efficiency-evelyn" and "soft-priority-lanes-burst-shaping-notes-sanjeev" docs for pattern overlaps; but this doc focuses on QPS skew impact on long-request tails.)
